STEP 4 OF 15
Hohmann's transfer: two burns

From a low orbit to geostationary height takes two burns. The first, along the direction of flight, stretches the circle into an ellipse whose far end reaches 35 786 km; half an orbit later, at the top, the second rounds it off. This is Walter Hohmann's transfer (1925), the cheapest two-burn way between two circles: from 500 km it costs about 3.8 km/s and takes a little over five hours.

STEP 5 OF 15
Molniya: slow at the top

A Soviet orbit for communications in the far north: a long ellipse whose apogee, 39 750 km up, is over the northern hemisphere. The coloured slices are equal times (Kepler's second law): the satellite rushes through its perigee in the south in under an hour and spends the other eleven of its twelve hours high over the north. At 63.4°, the critical inclination, the Earth's bulge does not turn the perigee, so the apogee stays in the north.

Each revolution the track steps west as the Earth turns beneath.

KEPLER'S LAWS
Kepler's first law

The orbit is an ellipse with the Earth's centre at one focus. This one has e = 0.7195, so the Earth's centre is 17,643 km from the middle of the ellipse.

Kepler's second law

The line from the Earth to the satellite sweeps equal areas in equal times — here 34,330 km² every second. So the satellite is fastest at perigee and slowest at apogee.

Kepler's third law

The square of the period over the cube of the semi-major axis is the same for every orbit of the Earth: T²/a³ = 9.904 × 10⁻⁵ s²/km³ (it is 4π²/μ). Here T = 10 h 37 min and a = 24,521 km.
